citation: U.S. Government Publishing Office (govinfo, U.S. Code link service). 10 U.S.C. 4022 — Authority of the Department of Defense to carry out certain prototype projects (2024 edition). n.d. https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/10/4022
date_note: No full date; sweep gives: 2024 edition (last amendment shown Pub. L. 118-159, Dec. 23, 2024).
publisher: U.S. Government Publishing Office (govinfo, U.S. Code link service)
summary: The prototype OT statute. Sets who may use the authority, the dollar tiers at which written determinations and congressional notice are needed, the four alternative conditions for using a prototype OT, Comptroller General access, definitions, and follow-on production. This edition predates Pub. L. 119-60, whose only change to the section text was a spelling correction (see usc-10-4022-lii).
why_it_mattered: 10 U.S.C. 4022 is the prototype Other Transaction authority: its four entry conditions and follow-on production clause are what make consortia and the innovation front doors work for small and nontraditional firms.
key_facts: (a)(1): DARPA Director, DIU Director, the Secretary of a military department, or any other official designated by the Secretary of Defense may carry out prototype projects under the authority of section 4021.

(a)(2)(A): over $100,000,000 but not over $500,000,000 (including all options) — written determination by the head of the contracting activity (or the director, for DARPA, DIU, MDA) that subsection (d) will be met and use of the authority is essential to promoting the success of the prototype project.

(a)(2)(B): over $500,000,000 (including all options) — senior procurement executive (or DARPA/DIU/MDA director) determines in writing that (d) will be met and use is essential to meet critical national security objectives; congressional defense committees notified in writing at least 30 days before the authority is exercised.

(a)(2)(C): follow-on production contract or transaction under (f) over $100,000,000 (including all options) — a covered official determines in writing that (d) was met for the prior prototype transaction, (f) will be met, and use is essential to meet critical national security objectives; congressional defense committees notified at the time the authority is exercised.
(a)(3): the determination authority under (a)(2) may not be delegated.
(b): section 4021(e)(2) (the research OT cost-share condition) does not apply; competitive procedures to be used to the maximum extent practicable.
(c): Comptroller General access clause for agreements providing payments over $5,000,000; limits for parties with no prior audit-access agreements; three-year limit on record examination.

(d)(1): one of four conditions must be met — (A) at least one nontraditional defense contractor or nonprofit research institution participating to a significant extent; (B) all significant participants other than the Federal Government are small businesses (including SBIR/STTR participants under 15 U.S.C. 638) or nontraditional defense contractors; (C) at least one third of the total cost paid from non-Federal sources; (D) the agency senior procurement executive determines in writing that exceptional circumstances justify the transaction.
(d)(2): costs incurred before the transaction's effective date do not count toward cost share, except costs incurred after negotiations began, on a written determination by the responsible official.

key_facts: Three types: Research OTs (10 U.S.C. 4021), Prototype OTs (10 U.S.C. 4022), Production OTs (10 U.S.C. 4022(f)).
OTs are not FAR-based procurement contracts, grants, cooperative agreements, or CRADAs (p. 5).
The FAR, the DFARS, DoD Source Selection Procedures and the Competition in Contracting Act do not apply to OT evaluation (p. 19).
Prototype OTs under § 4022 are Federal agency procurements for the Procurement Integrity Act (p. 14).

Still applicable matters it lists: property law when the Government takes title; FOIA with the five-year § 4021(i) protection; classified-information rules (32 CFR Part 117); DoDI 5200.48 for CUI; § 889 of the FY2019 NDAA.
"Successfully completed" means the performer met the key technical goals, satisfied the success metrics in the Prototype OT, or accomplished a particularly favorable or unexpected result (p. 16).
The solicitation and Prototype OT agreement should include notice that a follow-on Production OT is possible (p. 7).

Comptroller General access clause required for Prototype or follow-on production OTs with payments over $5 million; not required for Research OTs. Other audit and records access is negotiable; fixed-amount agreements generally need no audit provisions.
OTs are not subject to the Contract Disputes Act; the agreement should set its own dispute process, and counsel should advise on alternative dispute resolution (p. 22).
Protests: the Agreements Officer confers with counsel at once; agencies may set up an agency-level protest process and, if so, state it in the solicitation (p. 32).
IP: Agreements Officers should consult counsel and the DoD IP Cadre guidance; the Government has greater flexibility to negotiate IP terms than in traditional contracts (pp. 18–19).
Advertising: SAM.gov "may not be the most appropriate place" to advertise OT opportunities (pp. 11–12).
Each consortium member serving as the primary performer on an award must obtain a Unique Entity Identifier from SAM (p. 26).

Agreement terms discussed (II.E.3): price reasonableness, IP, physical property, disclosure and security, modifications, disputes, termination, follow-on production, recovery of funds, Government access, Comptroller General access, flow-down, accounting systems.
Payable milestones (III.M.1, p. 31); advance payments allowed (III.M.2); invoicing through WAWF in PIEE (III.M).

Government reports prototype and production OTs to FPDS; research OTs to FAADC (III.G).

summary: NIH's public OT policy guide. Old, but still posted. Lists small businesses among intended nontraditional partners.
key_facts: Dated May 22, 2017; Appendix 1 lists authorities, Appendix 2 lists laws that may not apply (including CICA and the Contract Disputes Act).
Names small businesses, patient advocacy organizations, educational institutions, pharmaceutical companies, foreign entities, consortia, nonprofits and individuals as possible partners.
Agreements Officers can negotiate IP terms that differ from other funding instruments.
Three payable-milestone options: fixed, adjustable (cost reimbursable), hybrid (II.K).
Cost sharing optional unless the program's legislation says otherwise; in-kind valued at fair market value (II.J.1).
Audits normally only when staff determine necessary (II.I).
quotes: Flexibility in the negotiation of IP rights is one of the rationales for using an OT.
There are three primary payable milestone options available for OTs: fixed, adjustable (cost reimbursable), and a hybrid approach
